senses: bluefin tuna, any of a number of types of tuna characterised by their blue fins.
To take off; take away, remove.
ety: From Middle English oftaken, equivalent to off- + take.

senses: A public hall or building for the use of visitors at health resorts or spas; a casino
ety: Borrowed from German Kursaal, from Kur (“cure”) + Saal (“hall”).
examples: Kursaal is a German word for casino, and a cosmopolitan term that became popular in the Belle Epoque.

senses: The carrying or transportation of goods by a porter (“person who carries luggage and related objects”) or other person.
Porters regarded collectively.
The charge for such carrying or transportation.
ety: From porter (“person who carries luggage and related objects”) + -age (suffix forming nouns indicating an action, process, or result; a charge, fee, or toll; or a relationship or state). Cognates * Anglo-Norman portage, porterage * Late Latin portagium

senses: A seminar conducted over a telephone, set up as a conference call.
resurrection, especially the resurrection of Jesus Christ
A two-masted fishing vessel, used by the Dutch until around the 18th century.
Conforming to God-rule, by Christian behavior.
Made of thin, beaten metal (of coins, ornaments etc. with a hollow underside).
ety: From Latin bracteātus (“gold-plated, golden”), from bractea (“gold leaf, veneer, glitter”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, bract + -eate (second element from -ea + -ate).

senses: An informal social gathering, especially one held over coffee for the purpose of conversation.
ety: Borrowed from German Klatsch (“meeting at which people gossip”).

senses: A chamber acting as the furnace in a jet engine or turbine engine, where intense combustion is induced.
ety: Borrowed from Latin combustor, from combūrō + -tor.

senses: The regeneration of a nerve's myelin sheath.
A person or thing that exchanges one thing for another.
A type of game controller held in both hands and controlled with the thumbs.
An unleavened bread in the cuisine of Libya prepared with barley, water and salt
A peer-to-peer network node which has the functionality of both server and client.
ety: Blend of server + client. Introduced by the Gnutella network technology.

senses: A Mexican ballroom and nightclub dance.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish cucaracha (“cockroach”). Doublet of cockroach.

senses: A Cuban cocktail, generally made from rum, lime, sugar, mint, etc.
ety: From Spanish mojito, diminutive of mojo (“sauce”), from mojar (“to moisten”), from Vulgar Latin *molliō (“to soften by soaking”), from Latin molliō (“soften”), from mollis (“soft”).

senses: A member of a Latin American gender role, variously construed as a cross-dressing man, a third gender or a trans woman.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish travesti and Portuguese travesti, themselves both from French travesti. Doublet of travesty.

senses: Given to grumbling
A thin, often flavored, Indian cigarette made of tobacco wrapped in a tendu leaf.
examples: I always write with the music on and a bottle of good red. And smoke Mangalore Ganesh beedies.
I walk in, talking to friendly faces in my aces / Drinking beer, smoking beedis in the back where the bass is

senses: Any of a group of various types of grass or its grains used as food, widely cultivated in the developing world.
ety: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French millet; from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μελίνη (melínē, “millet”) and Lithuanian málnos (“millet”). Not related to مِلَّة (milla).

senses: To combine parts to make a total.
To treat or construe something as universal, all-embracing, or comprehensive.
examples: She's heard me rant enough times about how transmasculine people get thrown under the bus in this kind of totalizing discourse, where any and all masculinity must be sacrificed at the altar of entry-level feminism

senses: The point, in any trajectory of an object in space, where it is closest to the Earth.
ety: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

senses: Synonym of pedophile.
Consisting of lines and simple shapes.
Having the stairs supported by the wall at one end only.
The branch of physiology dealing with the larynx and its disorders.
A rabbinic judge.
Paid a salary, as opposed to being an hourly worker or a volunteer. Generally indicating a professional or manager.
Paid monthly as opposed to weekly.
A feeling of identity and loyalty to one's tribe.
A person involved in the ownership or management of an industrial enterprise.
One who performs or enjoys industrial music.
examples: Brian Donlevy is a wealthy industrialist who survives an attempted murder when his wife's boyfriend is killed in a car crash.
Like a lot of second-wave industrialists, Skinny Puppy's attraction to rhythm wasn't consciously political, but based in the pleasure of making and moving to a beat; Key was, after all, a drummer.

senses: To make or become shaded or shady.
A drug for the treatment of late-stage melanoma.
A traditional Auvergne shepherd's hut with a thatched roof, or a rustic mountain chalet in the same style.
ety: Borrowed from French buron, from Middle French buron, from Old French buiron (“cabin, hut”), from Frankish *būr (“dwelling, residence”), from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“room, chamber, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to be, become, live, dwell”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Búur (“room, cage”), English bower, Swedish bur (“hutch, coop, cage”). Doublet of bower.
examples: According to Jaques, too, most of the tourists at the buron were French people with 'farming roots'

senses: Stamp collecting.
The study of postage stamps, postal routes, postal history, etc.
ety: First use appears c. 1865. Borrowed from French philatélie, coined by French stamp collector Georges Herpin in 1864 (in Le Collectionneur de Timbres-poste, Nov. 15, 1864), from Ancient Greek φιλέω (philéō, “I love”) + ἀτέλεια (atéleia), the closest word he could find in Ancient Greek to the concept of "postage stamp", from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + τέλος (télos, “tax”). This word serves as a reminder of the original function of postage stamps, now often forgotten: the cost of letter-carrying formerly was paid by the recipient; stamps indicated it had been prepaid by the sender, and thus the letters

senses: A conversation that takes place, usually in text, over the World Wide Web.
examples: Avon and Somerset Constabulary Interactive webchat (9 February 2007)

senses: A ring-shaped bread roll covered with sesame seeds.
ety: Borrowed from Turkish simit (“simit”), Ottoman Turkish سمید (simit), from Classical Persian سَمِید (samīd, “semolina”), from Arabic سَمِيد (samīd, “semolina”), from Aramaic סְמִידָא / ܣܡܻܝܕܳܐ (səmīḏā), from Akkadian 𒆠𒅔𒆠𒅔𒄯𒄯 (/⁠samīdu⁠/, “a type of fine groats, coarse flour, semolina”), related to Akkadian 𒀀𒊏𒄯𒄯 (/⁠samādu⁠/, “to grind fine”).

senses: Someone who plays a reed instrument.
examples: In Chicago he'll hook up with reedman Douglas Ewart, bassist Yosef ben Israel, and drummer Hamid Drake, and you can bet it won't be boring.

senses: A minced, cooked food (usually meat or vegetables), which is deep-fried in fat and sometimes sprinkled with breadcrumbs.
ety: Borrowed from French croquette, from croquer (“to crunch”) + -ette (suffix indicating diminution). Doublet of korokke.

senses: A sudden movement out of a straight line, for example to avoid a collision.
A deviation from duty or custom.
ety: From Middle English swerven, swarven, from Old English sweorfan (“to file; rub; polish; scour; turn aside”), from Proto-Germanic *swerbaną (“to rub off; wipe; mop”), from Proto-Indo-European *swerbʰ- (“to turn; wipe; sweep”). Cognate with West Frisian swerve (“to wander; roam; swerve”), Dutch zwerven (“to wander; stray; roam”), Low German swarven (“to swerve; wander; riot”), Swedish dialectal svärva (“to wipe”), Icelandic sverfa (“to file”).
